title: Every day is blessed
hook: the days, months and moments are blessed for those on whom grace falls (Barah Maha, ang 136)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the month of Phagun, and your line: phagun: bliss. Did you share one good thing with someone? The year of the Barah Maha has turned all the way round. Today it closes, with one short stanza about every day there is. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

People have always asked which days are lucky. Which date to marry on, which morning to sign the lease, which hour to start the journey. Calendars across the world are full of good days and bad ones. In Punjab, the first day of each solar month, when the sun moves into a new sign, is called Sangrand. On Sangrand many gurdwaras hold a special gathering, and the stanza of the Barah Maha for the new month is read aloud. So you might expect the poem to end by naming its best month. It doesn't.
screen: `WHICH DAYS ARE LUCKY?` → `SANGRAND: THE MONTH'S FIRST DAY.` → `THE POEM'S LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: The Barah Maha's closing stanza says, in paraphrase: the months, the days and the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. Nanak begs for the gift of Your sight; be merciful, Lord. Moorat, the word for moment, is the same word people use for an auspicious hour. And the stanza simply hands every hour to grace. No month in the poem is holy by itself. Chet isn't better than Poh. What makes a day blessed is whether it is lived in the Lord's sight. So Sikhs hold Sangrand in two ways, and both lean on this very stanza. Many keep it gladly: a monthly gathering, a reason to come to the gurdwara, a chance to hear the new month's stanza and begin again. Some Sikhs are wary of Sangrand becoming a lucky day, and point to this closing to say that no date carries power of its own. Both are trying to honor the same line. Now look back at the whole poem. It began with a year of longing, and a bride separated by her own deeds. Chet brought joy in remembering. Vaisakh, longing. Jeth, bowing. Asarh, keeping Him near in the heat. Sawan, blossoming. Bhadon, doubt. Assu, how to meet. Katak, blaming no one. Maghar, sitting together. Poh, held warm. Magh, the humble bath. Phagun, bliss. Twelve moods of one heart. And the last stanza says that every one of them, even the doubt, can be a blessed month. Every month is His.
screen: `MONTHS, DAYS, MOMENTS: BLESSED BY GRACE.` · `NO MONTH IS HOLY BY ITSELF.` · `TWO WAYS TO KEEP SANGRAND.` · `TWELVE MOODS OF ONE HEART.` · then, large: `EVERY MONTH IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the next Sangrand. Look up the date when the next Punjabi month begins, in a Sikh calendar or a gurdwara's notice, and put it in your diary. Write beside it the name of the month and its line from this block: Assu, how to meet; Poh, held warm; whichever comes next. Then sit with the breath, and let today count too, ordinary as it is. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Sangrand. The first day of a solar month, when gurdwaras read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha; and the poem's closing says every day is blessed when grace falls on it.

Your line: every month is his. Today, when you catch yourself calling it a bad day, add three words: still His day. Then see what changes. Tomorrow, a new voice: the ninth Guru. Day five hundred seventy-eight.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Sangrand, the Punjabi form of Sanskrit sankranti, the sun's passing into a new sign.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sangrand is a lucky day in the Sikh calendar.
what it means: it's the month's first day, a time to gather and hear the month's stanza; the poem itself says grace, not the date, makes a day blessed.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Barah Maha has fourteen stanzas, an opening, the twelve months and a closing, and the closing undoes the old calendar of lucky and unlucky days.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, closing stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136)
